style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings; 'the LORD' for YHWH; deity pronouns capitalized.
chapterNote: The oldest psalm in the book, a prayer of Moses the man of God -- almost certainly out of the wilderness years, while a whole generation died at the rate of the desert's funerals (Numbers 14). It sets the two clocks side by side. God's: from everlasting to everlasting, a thousand years passing like yesterday, like one watch of the night. Ours: swept off like a flood, a sleep, grass that sprouts at dawn and lies withered by dusk; seventy years, eighty with strength, and the best of them toil and sorrow before we fly away. Between the clocks stands the reason -- our iniquities set out in the light of His face, secret sins included, so that our days pass under wrath and end like a sigh. Out of that arithmetic rises the psalm's famous petition: teach us to number our days, that we may bring home a heart of wisdom. And then, remarkably, the old man in the desert asks for more than resignation -- satisfy us in the morning with Your covenant love; make us glad as many days as You afflicted us; let Your work appear, Your beauty rest on us, and the work of our hands, mortal as we are, be established by the Eternal. Establish it -- the prayer repeats -- yes, establish it.

1.text: A prayer of Moses, the man of God. Lord, You Yourself have been our dwelling place in generation after generation.
1.amp: A Prayer [tephillah] of Moses [Mosheh] the man [ish] of God [Elohim]. Lord [Adonai], You have been our dwelling place [maon -- habitation, refuge] in all generations ['in generation and generation', dor, the KJV margin].
1.notes: Prayed by a man who never had an address: forty years in Egypt, forty in Midian, forty in a tent moving through the desert -- and the confession is maon (H4583), home. The homeless generation's dwelling place was Adonai Himself, dor after dor (H1755).

2.text: Before the mountains were born, before You brought forth the earth and the world in birth-pangs, from everlasting to everlasting, You are God.
2.amp: Before the mountains [har] were brought forth [yalad -- born], or ever You had formed [chul -- writhed forth, as in birth-labor] the earth [eretz] and the world [tebel], even from everlasting [olam] to everlasting, You are God [El].
2.notes: Two birth-verbs for creation: yalad (H3205) and chul (H2342), the writhing of labor -- the mountains themselves are God's newborns. me-olam ad-olam (H5769): from the everlasting behind us to the everlasting ahead, one unbroken 'You are' -- El has no tenses.

3.text: You turn man back to crushed dust, and You say, 'Return, you children of Adam.'
3.amp: You turn [shub] man [enosh -- frail mortal man] to destruction [dakka -- crushed dust]; and say [amar], 'Return [shub], ye children [ben] of men [adam].'
3.notes: enosh (H582) is man in his frailty, and dakka (H1793) the crushed powder of Psalm 34:18 -- here the dust itself. The double shub (H7725) enforces Eden's sentence: dust you are, and to dust you shall return (cf. Genesis 3:19); death comes by spoken word, not blind process.

4.text: For a thousand years in Your sight are like yesterday once it has slipped past, like a single watch in the night.
4.amp: For a thousand [eleph] years [shanah] in Your sight [ayin] are but as yesterday [ethmol] when it is past [abar], and as a watch [ashmurah] in the night [layil].
4.notes: A millennium, measured at God's eye: one ethmol (H865), one yesterday already crossed -- or less, one ashmurah (H821), a four-hour night-watch a sleeper never even notices passing. Peter carries the verse into the New Testament's patience arithmetic (cf. 2 Peter 3:8).

5.text: You sweep them away like a flood; they become a sleep. In the morning they are like grass springing up new:
5.amp: You carry them away as with a flood [zaram]; they are as a sleep [shenah]: in the morning [boqer] they are like grass [chatsir] which grows up ['is changed', chalaph, the KJV margin].
5.notes: Three dissolving images in one verse: zaram (H2229), the flash-flood that scours a wadi; shenah (H8142), sleep that erases the hours; chatsir (H2682), the grass. chalaph (H2498) is to sprout anew and to pass on -- the same verb holding both halves of the grass's one-day life.

6.text: in the morning it blossoms and shoots up; by evening it is cut down and lies withered.
6.amp: In the morning [boqer] it flourishes [tsuts -- blossoms], and grows up [chalaph]; in the evening [erev] it is cut down [mul] and withers [yabesh].
6.notes: One day from tsuts (H6692), full flower, to yabesh (H3001), dried out: a human lifetime played at the desert's speed, where the morning's green is the evening's hay (cf. Isaiah 40:6-8; James 1:10-11). Moses watched it happen to a generation.

7.text: For we are consumed in Your anger, and by Your hot wrath we are terrified away.
7.amp: For we are consumed [kalah -- finished, spent] by Your anger [aph], and by Your wrath [chemah -- heat, fury] are we troubled [bahal -- dismayed, hurried away].
7.notes: The wilderness key: this is not death in the abstract but the sentence of Kadesh, a generation kalah (H3615), used up, under the aph and chemah (H639, H2534) their unbelief kindled (cf. Numbers 14:28-35). bahal (H926) is the panic of the hurried-off.

8.text: You have set our iniquities in front of You, our hidden sins in the full light of Your face.
8.amp: You have set [shith] our iniquities [avon] before You, our secret [alam -- hidden] sins in the light [maor] of Your countenance [panim].
8.notes: shith (H7896), deliberately placed: the avon (H5771) arranged on the desk before Him. alam (H5956) covers the sins hidden even from ourselves -- and the maor panim, the light of His face, which elsewhere blesses (cf. Numbers 6:25), here becomes the interrogation lamp nothing escapes.

9.text: For all our days turn away and decline under Your wrath; we finish our years like a sigh.
9.amp: For all our days [yom] are passed away ['turned away', panah, the KJV margin] in Your wrath [ebrah]: we spend [kalah -- finish] our years [shanah] as a tale that is told ['as a meditation', hegeh -- a murmur, a sigh].
9.notes: panah (H6437): the days turn their faces and leave. hegeh (H1899) is a low murmur, a sigh, a breath of sound -- seventy years compressed into the length of an exhale. kalah (H3615) again: the finishing-verb of verse 7 doing its slow daily work.

10.text: The days of our years come to seventy years, or eighty if strength holds, and even their best span is toil and sorrow, for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.
10.amp: The days [yom] of our years [shanah] are threescore years and ten [shibim -- seventy]; and if by reason of strength [geburah] they be fourscore [shemonim -- eighty] years, yet is their pride [rohab -- their best strength] labour [amal] and sorrow [aven]; for it is soon cut off [guz -- passes swiftly], and we fly away [uph].
10.notes: The famous audit: seventy, eighty with geburah (H1369) -- and Moses, who reached one hundred twenty, still counts the norm honestly. rohab (H7296), the proud best of those years, weighs out as amal and aven (H5999, H205), toil and trouble. guz (H1468), quickly cut -- and uph (H5774), the fly-away of a bird leaving a wire.

11.text: Who really knows the power of Your anger? Your wrath is as great as the fear that is owed You.
11.amp: Who knows [yada] the power [oz] of Your anger [aph]? even according to Your fear [yirah -- the reverence due You], so is Your wrath [ebrah].
11.notes: The unlearned lesson: no one takes the oz (H5797) of God's anger at its actual size -- it is proportioned to the yirah (H3374) He deserves, not the casual respect He receives. The question prepares the prayer of verse 12: since we cannot measure His wrath, let us at least measure our days.

12.text: So teach us to number our days, that we may bring home a heart of wisdom.
12.amp: So teach [yada -- make us know] us to number [manah] our days [yom], that we may apply ['cause to come', bo, the KJV margin] our hearts [lebab] unto wisdom [chokmah].
12.notes: The psalm's center. manah (H4487) is to count as a treasurer counts: days audited as the scarce currency they are. The Hebrew for 'apply' is bo, to bring in -- a harvest idiom: a lebab (H3824) of chokmah brought home like sheaves from a field that had only one growing season.

13.text: Return, O LORD -- how long? Have compassion on Your servants; let Your heart relent toward them.
13.amp: Return [shub], O LORD [YHWH], how long? and let it repent [nacham -- relent, be moved to compassion] You concerning Your servants [ebed].
13.notes: The turning-verb turned Godward: verse 3 commanded man to shub (H7725); now Moses dares to pray it back -- You return, LORD. nacham (H5162) is the relenting Moses had personally argued God into once before (cf. Exodus 32:12, 14); he prays here from experience.

14.text: Satisfy us in the morning with Your covenant love, and we will sing for joy and be glad through all our days.
14.amp: O satisfy [saba] us early [boqer -- in the morning] with Your mercy [chesed -- covenant love]; that we may rejoice [ranan -- ring out with joy] and be glad [samach] all our days [yom].
14.notes: The boqer (H1242) that belonged to the withering grass (v. 5-6) is re-petitioned for chesed (H2617): let the morning bring covenant love instead of the mower. saba (H7646), satisfied -- the one appetite seventy years cannot outlast -- and the gladness asked for covers 'all our days', the same days verse 9 sighed over.

15.text: Make us glad for as many days as You afflicted us, for as many years as we looked on evil.
15.amp: Make us glad [samach] according to the days [yom] wherein You have afflicted [anah] us, and the years [shanah] wherein we have seen [raah] evil [ra].
15.notes: The boldest arithmetic in the psalm: joy requested in the same units as the sorrow, day for day, shanah for shanah. anah (H6031) is the wilderness affliction itself (cf. Deuteronomy 8:2-3) -- and the prayer assumes the Judge of all the earth keeps accounts fine enough to match them.

16.text: Let Your work be seen by Your servants, and Your majesty by their children.
16.amp: Let Your work [poal] appear [raah] unto Your servants [ebed], and Your glory [hadar -- splendor, majesty] unto their children [ben].
16.notes: poal (H6467), God's own working: the dying generation asks to SEE it, and asks the hadar (H1926), the splendor, for their banim -- the children who would cross the Jordan they themselves would not. Faith's generosity: requesting for the next generation what it will not live to hold.

17.text: And let the beauty of the LORD our God rest upon us; establish the work of our hands upon us -- yes, the work of our hands, establish it.
17.amp: And let the beauty [noam -- the pleasantness, the delightfulness] of the LORD [YHWH] our God [Elohim] be upon us: and establish [kun -- make firm] You the work [maaseh] of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish You it.
17.notes: noam (H5278) is the beauty David longed to gaze on (cf. Psalm 27:4), here asked as a covering. And the closing doubled plea: kun (H3559), establish -- grass-brief creatures asking the everlasting God to give their maaseh (H4639) a permanence they themselves will never have. He answered: Moses' work stands to this hour, this psalm among it (cf. 1 Corinthians 15:58).
